1:
These two verses turn on two Hebrew words, and the versions disagree on both. Clarke lists what has been made of the first: sons of the strong ones, or sons of rams; the Chaldee's hosts of angels; the Greek and Latin reading bring to the Lord, ye sons of God, bring to the Lord the sons of rams. He quotes the old Psalter — bringes til Lord ye goddes sonnes, brynges til Lord sonnes of wether — glossed there as the hearers themselves, sons of apostles that were leaders of God's folk. Calvin explains how the confusion arose. The Greek translators rendered the phrase twice, as a vocative and as an accusative, apparently doubtful which was right and setting down both, and the Latin and the rest followed; but the correct rendering is ye sons of the mighty, a Hebrew idiom for ye princes.

Ellicott takes it more literally still: sons of gods, not sons of God, since the plural is never used by itself for God as the other divine name is. If it stands for beings of supernatural power inferior to God, angels is intelligible in the widest sense of ministers, including the lightning and the storm. On that reading the poet calls the forces of nature to praise their Master for the glory they were commissioned to reveal, and it is they who sing at both ends of the psalm.

Henry and Spurgeon both read the address as directed at rank. Henry hears it aimed at those who have power by succession, and notices the demand is made three times — intimating that the mighty are backward to this duty, though it matters greatly to God's kingdom that princes espouse it. What they give is first themselves and then their services: crowns laid at his feet, sceptres, swords, keys. Spurgeon presses harder. Neither men nor angels can confer anything on Jehovah; what men call natural causes are God in action, and the power must not be ascribed to them. Grandees often think it beneath them to fear the Lord, yet when brought to extol him their piety has been the greatest jewel in their crowns. Let all worship be to God only, emblazoned on every coat of arms. Calvin gives the reason for the special address: David meant to lead all men to worship, but since great men are hardest to reduce to order he addresses them expressly.

The occasion is disputed. Clarke collects the titles — the Latin dating the psalm to the completion of the tabernacle, the Greek to its going out, the Arabic calling it a prophecy of the incarnation — and guesses it commemorates the rain that fell in David's days after the heavens had been shut three years. Delitzsch grants the thunderstorm but will not stop there: the psalm is not limited to outward phenomena, since in it the God of redemptive history attests himself. He counts the voice of the Lord seven times, calls it the psalm of the seven thunders, and reports its place in the second Temple among the portions read at tabernacles.

The second word is the beauty of holiness, where the readings converge. Clarke makes it the beautiful garments of holiness, and would have priests and Levites put on their best apparel so that nothing in the service dishonours the divine majesty. Ellicott renders it holy attire from the same vestments, so that the presences attending the courts of heaven are bidden to robe themselves as for a high and sacred ceremony. Wesley keeps the house, not the dress. Gill glosses the glory due to the name as what suits God's nature; Clarke says what that nature is: his name is Mercy, his nature love. Augustine reads the address inward — bring yourselves, whom the apostles begot by the gospel, and worship in a heart enlarged and sanctified, since you are his royal and holy habitation.
3:
Ellicott reads the rest of the psalm as one storm tracked across a map. The invocation over, seven peals mark its course: first heard rolling over the waters from the west, it breaks on Lebanon, whose cedars, the mightiest and longest-lived of Eastern trees, crash down; the trees not snapped sway until they seem to bound like wild buffaloes, Sirion being the Sidonian name of Hermon and here the whole Anti-Lebanon range. No earthquake need be supposed, the apparent movement of the hills only heightening the violence. It then moves south and spends its last fury on the desert, where the striking thing is the whirlwind of sand — Stanley describing sheets of sand fleeting along the surface like streams of water, the air filled invisibly and driving in the face like sleet. It ends among the acacias and palms near Petra, discovereth meaning peels or strips.

Clarke reads the same events as physics. Thunder is called the voice of the Lord elsewhere in scripture; the many waters are the clouds, which Moses calls the waters above the firmament; and no agent in nature is so powerful as the electric fluid, which rends the strongest oaks and cleaves solid rock. On the hinds he is brief: the storm strikes terror through all the tribes of animals, which sometimes causes the pregnant to cast their young, and this he believes is the whole the text means — he will not meddle with the fables published by ancients and moderns.

Gill takes every clause twice, the second time allegorically. The voice on the waters is Christ's voice in the gospel reaching many peoples; the flames of fire are the cloven tongues at Pentecost, or the gospel hewing down the goodliness of men; the shaken wilderness is the Gentile world, whose minds the preaching shook till they cried what shall we do to be saved; and the hinds that calve are churches and ministers by whom souls are brought forth to Christ. He keeps the plain sense too: hinds bear their young when thunder is most frequent.

What the word rendered voice carries is disputed. Delitzsch reports that it is sometimes an ejaculation, no more than Hark, but refuses that here, since the psalm's theme is the voice of God announcing himself from heaven; the dull sound denotes not only thunder but the roar of the tempest and of the earthquake besides. Ellicott sets out both views and prefers a third: not thunder alone but the combined noise of thunder, wind and rain — the gods, in Shakespeare's phrase, that keep this pudder over our heads. Wesley keeps to short glosses: the waters are the clouds, and Lebanon and Sirion skip by poetical hyperbole.

At the end the storm is over and the throne appears. Ellicott renders it Jehovah was throned upon the flood, the word being used nowhere else except of the Deluge, so the torrents of rain must have recalled the poet to it — or it had become proverbial for any great rain. Clarke has Jehovah sitting on the deluge after the confusion, appeasing the fury of the jarring elements, and prints beside it Virgil's Neptune calming the sea Juno raised against the fleet of Aeneas, asking whether the Roman borrowed his chief ideas from this psalm. Delitzsch records Luther's attempt — the Lord sitteth to prepare a Flood — as an effort to make sense of an unintelligible Latin and Greek. Of the last verse Ellicott says only that it looks like a liturgical addition giving the poem a religious tone; Spurgeon takes it for the whole point, since the power displayed in the hurricane is now promised as the strength of the chosen, and he who wings the unerring bolt will give his redeemed the wings of eagles. Is not this a noble psalm to sing in stormy weather, he asks — can you sing amid the thunder?
